full_judgment:
20. As to the other witnesses, P.W. 4 has admitted that he is an accused in a case filed by appellant Shah Alam. P.W.2 has admitted that he brought a criminal case against his cousin Kalam in which Informant (P.W.1) is his witness; as such, he is under obligation to depose in this case filed by P.W.1. P.Ws 4 and 7 are both first cousins of P.W.5 and the deceased and as such are interested witnesses. P.W.7 Kabir Ahmed (son of Hedayet) admitted that he was an accused in a dacoity case but explained that he was acquitted; he, however, denied that he got the acquittal by compromise by giving 3 kanis of land to Shah Alam. P.W. 11 is brother-in-law of P.W.7. As to P.W. 10 he denied the suggestion that he along with P.Ws. 4, 5, 7 and Abdul Karim Chowdhury are accused in still another caser-C.R. Case No. 437 of 1976-filed by Shah Alarn's relation Abdus Sabur. Shah Alam, however, filed papers of that case as a part of his statement under s.342 Cr.P.C. It is clear that the persons who came to depose against the accused are all interested witnesses and none of them is independent having no grudge with the accused. Even those among them who deposed as to what they heard immediately after the incident are also not disinterested. It is in evidence that just after the incident 50 to 60 persons came to the dead body at the Bhanga and over 100 persons came when the dead body was removed to his house, but none of them has been examined as a witness except these very witnesses from the Bhanga. Even the wife of the deceased was not examined. In a criminal case, a per- son who hears about an incident immediately after it occurs is also a competent witness to say as to what he has heard from those who claimed to have seen it. Wife of the decessed could have at least said as to what she had heard about the murder of her husband when the dead body was brought to her, as the witnesses said, within a very short time. She could have also said whether her husband had gone to the Hat from where he was returning home without any "marketing", as P.W.1 said, for it might be that her f husband did not go to the Hat, but went to the Bhanga after 'dusk for some other business. Siraj's son Rafiquddin, though cited as witness in the Charge- sheet, has not been examined. In the circumstances, it appears, they, mother and son, have been kept out of the way so that some unpleasant truth could not come out; the Court is therefore justified to draw an adverse presumption against the prosecution for non- examination of competent witnesses without giving any reason. 

 38. "Sections 417, 418 and 423 of the Code give to the High Court full power to review at large the evidence upon which the order of acquittal was founded, and to reach the conclusion that upon that evidence the order of acquittal should be reversed. No limitation should be placed upon that power, unless it be found expressly stated in the Code. But in exercising the power conferred by the Code and before reaching its conclusions upon fact the High Court should and will always give proper weight and consideration to such matters as (1) the views of the trial Judge as to the credibility of the witnesses; (2) the presumption of innocence in favour of the accused, a presumption certainly not weakened by the fact that he has been acquitted at his trial; (3) the right of the accused to the benefit of any doubt; and (4) the slowness of an appellate Court in disturbing a finding of fact arrived at by a Judge who had the ad-vantage of seeing the witnesses. To state this however is only to say that the High Court in its con-duct of the appeal should and will act in accordance with rules and principles well known and recognized in the administration of justice".
